value: The region's flagship grape, best known for dry wines that can age for many years.
source_notes: Wine Folly: flagship, high quality age worthy dry Riesling is the specialty. Fortune: region made its name with Riesling, which leads plantings by far.

value: Taut and high in acidity, with citrus and green apple fruit and a stony, slatey feel on the palate.
source_notes: Wine Folly: dry Riesling with green apple, lemon, lime, racy acidity. James Suckling: classic acidity, citrus, focused, slatey feeling on the palate.

value: The leading red grape of the region, prized for coping with its cold winters.
source_notes: Wine & Spirits: most planted red, the red standard bearer, promoted because like Riesling it tolerates severe cold. Fortune: most planted vinifera red, the darling red grape of the state.

value: Fresh and supple, with red and dark fruit and a light peppery, herbal edge closer to the Loire than to California.
source_notes: Wine & Spirits: supple, red fruited, mild herbal edge, resembles the reds of the central Loire. Wine Folly: blackberry, a hint of pepper and violet, ripe plum.

value: Grown in small amounts, both for still red wine and, with Chardonnay, for traditional method sparkling wine.
source_notes: Fortune: Pinot Noir plantings are limited and growers are less keen because of low yields. Wine Folly: Champagne style sparkling made with Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

value: Lighter and leaner than West Coast Pinot Noir, with moderate alcohol and bright, noticeable acidity.
source_notes: Fortune: lacks the power of California Pinot, balanced, moderate alcohol, edge of acid. VinePair: leaner, lighter coloured, Burgundian rather than Sonoma, refreshing acidity. Decanter (premium, snippet only): cool climate expression with noticeable acidity in contrast to the West Coast.

value: The region's flagship red grape, made on its own and as the base of Bordeaux style blends.
source_notes: Wine Folly: flagship tends to be Bordeaux varieties such as Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon. NorthForker: best wines made from Merlot and Cabernet Franc; Long Island Merlot as a regional identity.

value: Fresher and more savoury than warm climate Merlot, with black fruit, bright acidity and firm tannins.
source_notes: Wine Folly: Bordeaux style blends show fresh black fruit, savoury finish, high acidity, grippy just ripe tannins. Wine Enthusiast review of a North Fork Merlot: black plum with leafy, gamey hints.

value: One of the region's flagship reds, made on its own, in Bordeaux style blends and as the usual base for dry rosé.
source_notes: Wine Folly: flagship Bordeaux variety; dry rosé normally based on Cabernet Franc. VinePair: trade group promotes Sauvignon Blanc and Cabernet Franc as grapes that do especially well. NorthForker: best wines from Merlot and Cabernet Franc.

value: Planted in the region's first vineyards and one of the grapes behind its Bordeaux style reds.
source_notes: Vinography: planted by the Hargraves in the first commercial vineyard; early success with cabernet thanks to the long season. Wine Folly: one of the flagship Bordeaux varieties.

value: Crisp and restrained, with green apple and citrus, and usually less oak and butter than other American Chardonnay.
source_notes: Wine Folly: restrained, less oak and buttery character than many US regions, a salty quality. VinePair: crisp and balanced, green apple, zesty acidity, subtle oak.

value: Grown since the region's first vineyards and seen by its growers as one of the grapes best suited to it.
source_notes: Vinography: among the Hargraves' original plantings. VinePair: trade group promotes Sauvignon Blanc and Cabernet Franc as grapes that do especially well here.

value: Crisp, with citrus and a saline edge, closer to the Loire than to the greener New Zealand style.
source_notes: VinePair: leans toward Loire styles, far less green and herbaceous than New Zealand. NorthForker: citrus and pear, bright acidity, distinct saline minerality.

value: Used with Chardonnay in the region's traditional method sparkling wines, as well as for some still red.
source_notes: Wine Folly: traditional method sparkling with Chardonnay and Pinot Noir is a major focus. Wine Spectator listing of a North Fork traditional method Brut (Sparkling Pointe) made from Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

value: The leading red grape of the area, usually made as a dry varietal red and sometimes blended into Bordeaux style reds.
source_notes: Wine Folly: Cabernet Franc is the most planted grape in Virginia, usually a dry oaked varietal, also blended into Meritage; Monticello noted for Cabernet Franc. VinePair: Cabernet Franc does phenomenally well in Virginia. Both are statewide, not Monticello specific.

value: A signature white of the area, usually made dry.
source_notes: Wine Folly: one of Virginia's signature grapes, typically dry; Monticello produces high quality Viognier. Wine with Seth (blog): Viognier is the signature white of the Monticello AVA.

value: Widely grown and made in styles that run from lean, unoaked wines to richer barrel aged ones.
source_notes: Wine Folly: style varies by winery, often oaked with malolactic, but can be lean, fresh and steely; Monticello named for Chardonnay. Firstleaf (retailer) Monticello page: Chardonnay ranges from fresh unoaked to richer barrel aged.

value: The grape that defines the region, with many very old, head trained vines still in production.
source_notes: Wine Folly: the one grape that defines Lodi, most widely planted, many century old head trained vines saved by Zinfandel. Lodi Winegrape Commission: explains old vine single vineyard Lodi wines, most vines at least fifty years old.

value: Ripe, bold and fruit forward here, usually full bodied with a peppery spice.
source_notes: Wine Folly: Lodi's bold, fruit forward style; rich, fruity, somewhat smoky. Lodi Winegrape Commission: fruity, peppery spiced, zesty, full bodied characteristics; alcohol mostly 14 to 16 percent.

value: Widely grown here, much of it for the value priced California wines of large brands.
source_notes: Lodi Winegrape Commission (growers site): Lodi produces more Cabernet than any other US region; most of the industry's value priced Cabernet is grown there. Wine Folly: several large brands use Lodi Cabernet, Chardonnay, Merlot, Pinot Grigio for California wines.

value: The region's signature grape, with many very old, ungrafted vines, most of them in Amador County.
source_notes: Decanter (search snippet; full page not retrievable): best known region is Amador, where most old Zinfandel vineyards are; centenarian vineyards not uncommon; old vines on own roots. Wine & Spirits Magazine: Amador Zinfandel history, vines ungrafted and unirrigated, old head trained vines.

value: One of the region's signature red grapes, grown above all in Amador County.
source_notes: Dan Berger column (Napa Valley Focus): largest Barbera plantings in California are in the Sierra Foothills, notably Amador County. Firstleaf (wine club guide): Barbera a signature variety of the region, Sobon Estate in Amador noted.

value: Grown in both El Dorado and Amador counties, on granite and volcanic hillside soils.
source_notes: El Dorado Winery Association: Syrah a regional staple, links elevation and granite soils, Lava Cap Syrah on volcanic soil. Decanter (paywalled, search snippet only): the two counties produce a range of Syrah styles from powerful to delicate.

value: One of the region's oldest grapes, and some of California's largest stands of old Zinfandel vines still produce here, many on the west side.
source_notes: Paso Robles Wine Country Alliance: among the region's earliest plantings; Dusi family old head pruned Zinfandel still in production. Zinfandel Advocates and Producers: perhaps one of the highest concentrations of old vine Zinfandel vineyards; Dusi on the west side. Wine Folly: first commercially viable grape planted in Paso.

value: Some of California's first modern Syrah was planted here, and it is a leading grape of the region's Rhône style reds, bottled alone and in blends.
source_notes: Paso Robles Wine Country Alliance: first modern commercial acreage of Syrah in the state. Wine Spectator: Estrella clone planted in Paso widely considered the founding clone of California Syrah. Wine Folly: largest Syrah acreage in California, Rhone Zone, Syrah in Rhone style blends.

value: A main grape of the region's Rhône style reds, usually leading blends with Syrah and Mourvèdre, and favoured in the cooler western hills.
source_notes: Wine Folly: red Rhone wines traditionally Grenache dominated blends with Syrah and Mourvedre; western hilly areas suit Rhone varieties. Wine Spectator: Rhone varieties lead in Adelaida District, often planted in Willow Creek. PBS SoCal: Tablas Creek plants Grenache on west side limestone, blends Syrah, Grenache, Mourvedre.

value: Usually big, ripe and richly textured, softer and more opulent than many Napa Cabernets.
source_notes: Wine Folly: Paso style is big and bold, richly textured, opulent, ready drinking Cabernets. Wine Spectator: in warm San Juan Creek expect big, bold, ripe wines (not Cabernet specific). LCBO (search snippet, page 403): many of the finest Cabs richer and darker than Napa's. A producer quoted elsewhere says there is no single Paso style.

value: Made across a wide range here, from fresh, crisp and lively to rich, round and buttery, depending largely on the winemaking.
source_notes: Visit Napa Valley: styles range from fresh, crisp and lively to rich, round and buttery. Napa Valley Vintners grape guide (read via search snippet, page returned 403): spans fresh and lively to richer and buttery, mainly through barrel fermentation, lees stirring and malolactic choices; does best in cool Carneros.

value: Long established in the valley, on sites such as Stags Leap District and the cooler Carneros, and made in styles from medium bodied with fresh red fruit to full bodied and rich.
source_notes: Visit Napa Valley: a fixture in the valley since the early 1970s; varied sites allow lighter and full bodied versions. NAPA Magazine (Napa Valley Vintners): Clos Du Val grows Merlot in Stags Leap District and Carneros; valley Merlots range from intense full bodied to medium bodied with fresh red fruit.

value: Softer and silkier than the valley's Cabernet Sauvignon, with a smooth finish and a ripe, fruit forward feel.
source_notes: Visit Napa Valley: ripe cherry, rich earthiness, soft texture and smooth finish. NAPA Magazine (Napa Valley Vintners): Miner's winemaker calls Merlot silkier, softer and more fruit forward than Cabernet; Carneros Merlot more fruit forward and fresh.

value: One of the valley's two main grapes, alongside Pinot Noir, and grown widely across its fog cooled vineyards.
source_notes: Russian River Valley Winegrowers: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir are the two varieties the region suits best; Chardonnay the largest share of the harvest; climate page: onshore breezes and fog cool the vineyards. Sonoma County Tourism: world famous for its Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Wine Folly: famous for Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

value: Generous in texture yet kept fresh and lively by bright citrus acidity, which the valley's cool nights and fog help preserve.
source_notes: Russian River Valley Winegrowers: fog and the daily temperature swing preserve acidity and aromas. Wine Enthusiast reviews of single wines: rich structure with zesty acid; zippy lemon tangerine acidity. Lynmar Estate (producer): bright citrus, liveliness and freshness, generous mouthfeel that never tips into heaviness.

value: One of the valley's two main grapes, alongside Chardonnay; the cool Green Valley area within it is especially known for it.
source_notes: Russian River Valley Winegrowers: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are the two varieties the region suits best. Wine Folly: Russian River Valley famous for Pinot Noir; Green Valley sub AVA known for Pinot Noir. Sonoma County Winegrowers: Green Valley is a cooler Pinot neighborhood.

value: Generally plump, rich and fruit forward, with a velvety texture held in balance by fresh acidity.
source_notes: Wine Spectator: Russian River generally produces plump, rich and fruit forward Pinots. Wine Folly: typically lighter in color with a velvety texture; high acidity balances lush fruit.

value: Livelier in acidity than Zinfandel from hotter places, with wild berry fruit and a pronounced spiciness.
source_notes: Sonoma County Winegrowers: winemakers get higher acid levels from many Santa Rosa Plain old vine sites, with wild berry flavors and pronounced spice. Russian River Valley Winegrowers: cool climate Zinfandel offers a counter style to the same grapes from hotter regions; Santa Rosa Plain Zinfandels are spicy and raspberry influenced.

value: Gentle and silky in tannin, soft on the palate rather than firm, with fresh fruit kept lively by good acidity.
source_notes: Sonoma County Winegrowers: Alexander Valley Cabernet relatively soft on the palate, silky tannins, acidity and freshness balance fruit and tannin. Wine & Spirits Magazine: silken, gentle tannins, fresh black currant flavor and textural finesse.

value: Varies with the site, from firm, high acid wines on the cool coast to richer, fuller ones from warm inland valleys such as Alexander Valley.
source_notes: Sonoma County Tourism: cooler coastal areas like the Sonoma Coast build acidity and structure; the warmest areas, Alexander and Knights Valley, also make excellent Chardonnay. Wine Folly: Alexander Valley known for richly flavored Chardonnays; Chalk Hill more Chablis like.

value: From the highest coastal sites it is leaner and firmer, with an earthy edge and a dense core of acidity.
source_notes: Wine Spectator: the best, highest elevation Sonoma Coast vineyards make Pinots with appealing earthiness and a dense core of tannins and acidity. Wine Folly: Fort Ross Seaview, in the Sonoma Coast, makes distinctly leaner Pinots with chalky minerality.

value: Often brambly and strongly spiced, with old vines giving small berries and concentrated flavor.
source_notes: Sonoma County Winegrowers: older vines produce small berries and clusters with intensity of flavor; pronounced spice on Santa Rosa Plain. Wine Enthusiast single wine reviews (Dry Creek Valley): enormously spicy, briary and brambly; spicy and intense from pre Prohibition vines.

value: Grown mainly on the warmer slopes facing San Francisco Bay, where Monte Bello Ridge is its best known site.
source_notes: K&L Wines (retailer): warmer interior Bay side suits Bordeaux varieties, Cabernet examples Ridge Monte Bello, Mount Eden, Fellom Ranch all Bay side. Ridge Vineyards (producer): Monte Bello is its Cabernet site within the AVA, eastern slope toward the Bay.

value: Firmer and leaner than most California Cabernet, with firm acidity and a mineral streak that suits long ageing.
source_notes: Ridge Vineyards (producer): regional hallmarks are structured tannins, firm acidity, a streak of minerality, long ageing. Sunset magazine: Monte Bello shows firm acids and bright fruit grounded in limestone.

value: Grown mainly on the cool slopes facing the Pacific, where ocean fog slows ripening.
source_notes: K&L Wines (retailer): Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are on the ocean side, tempered by the Pacific, Monterey Bay and persistent fog. Sunset: Chardonnay on mountain slopes where cool foggy conditions slow ripening.

value: Leaner and livelier than most California Chardonnay, with high acidity and a stony, salty edge.
source_notes: Sunset: Bargetto, Cinnabar, Mount Eden Chardonnays lively, lean, stony; ocean air keeps acidity high. K&L Wines: racy, fresh, saline, mouthwatering acidity. Mississippi Free Press: minerality and acidity temper the fruit.

value: Grown mainly on the cool slopes facing the Pacific, often in fog, alongside Chardonnay.
source_notes: K&L Wines (retailer): Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are on the ocean side with persistent fog. Sunset: Pinot Noir among the region's cool weather stars.

value: The main grape of the Highlands, where strong afternoon winds off Monterey Bay give a long growing season.
source_notes: Santa Lucia Highlands Wine Artisans: Pinot Noir is the flagship. Wine Industry Advisor: Pinot and Chardonnay dominate plantings; afternoon winds allow long hang time.

value: Riper and fuller than most cool coast Pinot Noir, with dark cherry fruit and firm tannins from wind thickened skins, yet still bright in acidity.
source_notes: SLH Wine Artisans: rich, silky, dark cherry and raspberry, earth, bright acidity. Wine Industry Advisor: robust structure, thicker skins from wind, retained acidity with ripe tannins. Siduri (producer): ripe flavour and weight with electric acidity from long hang time.

value: The second grape after Pinot Noir, grown across the slopes and made in styles from crisp to rich.
source_notes: SLH Wine Artisans: grown across the appellation, styles from crisp to opulent. Wine Industry Advisor: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay dominate plantings.

value: Rich and often tropical in fruit, yet kept fresh by acidity held through the long, windy season.
source_notes: SLH Wine Artisans: balance of tropical richness and precision, lively acidity. Wine Industry Advisor: winemakers call it very tropical, rich and viscous; long season and cold winds combine ripeness with acidity.

value: A minor grape beside Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, grown by a small number of producers.
source_notes: SLH Wine Artisans: one of the other varieties a growing number of producers explore. Wine Industry Advisor: among the minor plantings. Market Watch: Morgan, Manzoni, Franscioni, Hahn, Paraiso grow it.

value: A cool climate style, savoury and peppery rather than ripe and jammy.
source_notes: SLH Wine Artisans: peppery, savory Syrah. Market Watch: producer Mark Manzoni calls his a cool climate Syrah in an Old World style, not sweet or jammy.

value: A minor grape beside Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, grown by a handful of producers.
source_notes: SLH Wine Artisans: an emerging cool climate variety. Wine Industry Advisor: among minor plantings. Market Watch: Morgan, Franscioni, Hahn, Paraiso have plantings.

value: One of the valley's two main grapes with Chardonnay, grown in a long, cool season as Pacific fog and wind funnel up the valley.
source_notes: GuildSomm: primary varieties Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Wine Folly: first Santa Barbara region planted to Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, funnel shaped, longest growing season. BBR: one of the two most prominent grapes, cool ocean influenced climate.

value: Darker and more savoury than many coastal California Pinot Noirs, with spice and earthy notes under the cherry fruit.
source_notes: Wine Folly: highly aromatic, spice, undertone of savory meat, powerful structure. GuildSomm: moodier, darker cherry with earthy spice and tea. (BBR says bright red fruit, so not unanimous.)

value: One of the valley's two main grapes with Pinot Noir, and among the first grapes planted in Santa Barbara County.
source_notes: Wine Folly: first region in Santa Barbara to plant Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. GuildSomm: primary varieties Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. BBR: one of the leading grapes.

value: Fresh and firm in acidity, with citrus and orchard fruit, leanest toward the cool western end of the valley.
source_notes: Wine Folly: lemon zest, nectarine, pear, firm acidity. GuildSomm: far west lean with bright acidity and green apple, eastern benches fuller. BBR: crisp acidity.

value: A smaller third grape after Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, made here in a cool climate style.
source_notes: GuildSomm: primary Pinot Noir and Chardonnay with a good portion of Syrah. Wine Folly: Syrah in a more Northern Rhone style than a Californian one.

value: Leaner, more peppery and more savoury than most California Syrah, closer in feel to the northern Rhone.
source_notes: Wine Folly: meaty, tobacco and spice notes, more Northern Rhone style than Californian. Wine Review Online (single bottle review, Presqu'ile): cool climate sense of place, emphasis on pepper and herbs.

value: The main grape, grown in a cold, windy corridor between two ranges of hills that opens straight onto the Pacific.
source_notes: GuildSomm: Pinot Noir the most planted grape. Wine Folly: Pinot Noirs dominate; marine layer, windy. Sta. Rita Hills Wine Alliance: planted with Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, east west maritime throat, fog and wind.

value: Deeper in colour and more concentrated than its cool climate suggests, while keeping a firm, nervy line of acidity.
source_notes: Wine Folly: dark fruited (plum, black cherry), highly concentrated. Wine and Spirits: Pinot can be dark and dense, western bluffs give nervy bottlings. (GuildSomm instead stresses bright red cherry.)

value: The second grape after Pinot Noir, grown in the same cool, wind swept sites.
source_notes: GuildSomm: Chardonnay second most planted after Pinot Noir. Wine Folly: Pinot Noir dominates, followed by Chardonnay. Wine Alliance: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay the main plantings.

value: Taut and racy, with pronounced acidity and lemon or green apple fruit rather than the richer tropical style of warmer California.
source_notes: Wine Folly: taut, racy Chardonnays. GuildSomm: lemon, green apple or yellow apple fruit, some sites mineral.

value: A smaller grape here, first planted on the warmer east side and now also grown toward the colder western edge.
source_notes: Wine and Spirits: early Syrah plantings mostly on the warmer east side, growers moved west for cooler sources. GuildSomm: Syrah among the other grapes after Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

value: Lean, savoury and peppery, with a tense cool climate feel closer to the northern Rhone than to riper California Syrah.
source_notes: Wine and Spirits: savory, aromatic, nervy and edgy, likened to Cote Rotie, more tense and savory further west. GuildSomm: some Syrah lean, often with whole cluster spice.

value: One of the valley's main grapes, grown alongside Merlot and Syrah in a valley planted overwhelmingly to red varieties. Cooler sites toward the Blue Mountains and higher up suit it best.
source_notes: Washington State Wine: top varieties Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah; production dominated by red varieties. Wine Folly: Cabernet Sauvignon a main variety; moving east toward the Blue Mountains or up in elevation brings cooler temperatures that suit Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Malbec. Visit Walla Walla: Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah and Merlot make up more than half of plantings.

value: One of the valley's main red grapes, grown alongside Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah, and suited to the cooler sites toward the Blue Mountains.
source_notes: Washington State Wine: Merlot among top varieties. Wine Folly: cooler eastern and higher sites suit Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Malbec; climate makes refined Merlot. Visit Walla Walla: Merlot one of the three grapes making up more than half of plantings.

value: An established red grape here, grown alongside Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah among the valley's leading varieties.
source_notes: Visit Walla Walla: top five varietals are Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Malbec. Great Northwest Wine (Herald): red varieties lead, with cabernet sauvignon, merlot, syrah and cabernet franc.

value: Savory and meaty here, with dark plum and blackberry joined by black olive and smoked meat notes, plusher still from the cobbled soils of The Rocks District.
source_notes: Wine Folly: Walla Walla Syrah noted for juicy plum, savory blackberry and meaty notes of black olive and bacon; wines from The Rocks have a more plush style with roasted meat and game. Oregon Wine Board (Rocks District AVA page): Syrah predominant; wines show a perfumed bouquet with a savory palate.

value: The valley's signature grape, on which its reputation was built, grown across its hillsides from the first plantings onward.
source_notes: Willamette Valley Wineries Association: Pinot noir is the valley's hallmark; pioneers planted the first Pinot noir and Chardonnay. Oregon Wine Board: Pinot noir is Oregon's flagship variety with particular prominence in the Willamette Valley.

value: The valley's leading white grape, made by most Pinot Noir producers in styles from crisp and light to rich and full bodied.
source_notes: Oregon Wine Board: Pinot gris found mainly in the Willamette Valley and Southern Oregon, planted on twice the share of Chardonnay; can be crisp and light or rich and full bodied. Prince of Pinot: most widely planted Oregon white; practically every major Oregon Pinot Noir producer releases a Pinot Gris.

value: Fuller and more fruit driven than most Italian Pinot Grigio yet usually drier than Alsace, with citrus and light floral notes.
source_notes: Oregon Wine Board: follows an Alsatian style of vinification; fragrant, lightly floral with citrus. Prince of Pinot: more fruit, weight and structure than most Italian Pinot Grigio; not often perceived as sweet as many Alsatian versions.

value: Planted alongside Pinot Noir by the valley's first growers and now a rising grape here, made as still and sparkling wine.
source_notes: Willamette Valley Wineries Association: early families planted the first Pinot noir and Chardonnay; wineries make Chardonnay as still and sparkling wines; Chardonnay a silent partner now ready for recognition. Oregon Wine Board: Chardonnay rapidly growing in popularity, mainly in the Willamette Valley and Rogue Valley.

value: Taut and fresh, with high natural acidity and restrained oak, and often compared with white Burgundy.
source_notes: GuildSomm: cool climate gives high natural acidity; moderate new oak; many similarities with white Burgundy. Willamette Valley Wineries Association: acidity from the cool climate makes it sing; winemaking about restraint; one wine likened to Meursault.

value: The valley's main grape, made as still red wine and, picked early, as traditional method sparkling wine.
source_notes: Anderson Valley Winegrowers Association: one of the most celebrated grapes, early picked clusters used for Blanc de Noirs and traditional method sparkling | Wine Anorak (Jamie Goode): Pinot Noir the main focus, sparkling a star of the valley | Wine Folly: Pinot, Chardonnay and sparkling are the standout wines

value: Bright and fresh here, with lively acidity, red fruit and moderate alcohol from the cool, foggy valley.
source_notes: Anderson Valley Winegrowers Association: bright natural acidity, silky tannins, wild berry, red cherry, pomegranate; cool maritime climate and fog | Wine Folly: high acidity and lower alcohol, around 13.5%, from cooler conditions

value: Grown mostly alongside Pinot Noir, for still white wine and, with Pinot Noir, for traditional method sparkling wine.
source_notes: Wine Anorak: Chardonnay a strong performer, mostly paired with Pinot Noir for sparkling | Wine Folly: Pinot, Chardonnay and sparkling wines are the valley's standout expressions

value: One of the first grapes planted in the valley, and made in styles from bone dry to late harvest sweet.
source_notes: Anderson Valley Winegrowers Association: grown in the valley since the 1960s, styles range from bone dry to late harvest dessert wines | Press Democrat / North Bay Business Journal: first planted in the valley by Donald Edmeades in 1964; ranges from sweet to dry, dry versions sold well

value: Lighter and crisper here than in warmer places, and usually made dry or off dry.
source_notes: Anderson Valley Winegrowers Association: palate surprisingly crisp and vibrant, often dry or off dry | Wine Folly: the cool climate is ideal for lighter, sharper grapes like Riesling and Gewürztraminer | Press Democrat: grapes from too warm areas turn bitter; dry versions from Navarro and Husch

value: A grape from the valley's early years that has largely been grafted over to Pinot Noir, so only a few plantings remain.
source_notes: Wine Anorak: Riesling was a large share of plantings in the early days, vines grafted over to Pinot Noir | Press Democrat: only four riesling plantings in the valley; Navarro still makes it

value: A leading red grape across the valley, most important on warm, dry sites such as Red Mountain and the Wahluke Slope.
source_notes: Wine Folly: Cabernet Sauvignon the state's top grape; Red Mountain dark tannic reds, Wahluke Slope Cabernet | Washington State Wine: Columbia Valley top varieties begin with Cabernet Sauvignon; Red Mountain dominated by Cabernet; Wahluke Slope one of the warmest appellations, Cabernet first among top varieties

value: Grown widely alongside Cabernet Sauvignon, with warm sites such as Red Mountain and the Wahluke Slope among its homes.
source_notes: Wine Folly: Merlot grown in Yakima Valley, Red Mountain, Horse Heaven Hills, Wahluke Slope, Rattlesnake Hills | Washington State Wine: Merlot among top varieties of Columbia Valley, Red Mountain and Wahluke Slope

value: A red grape of growing standing here, grown on Red Mountain and in the Horse Heaven Hills among other sites.
source_notes: Wine Folly: amazing potential in the Columbia Valley; Horse Heaven Hills known for it; Red Mountain Syrah | Washington State Wine: Syrah a top variety of Red Mountain | Decanter (search snippet only): Syrah may have finally found its footing in the Columbia Valley

value: One of the grapes the valley first became known for, made in styles from dry to late harvest sweet, with cooler areas such as the Yakima Valley and Ancient Lakes best suited.
source_notes: Wine Folly: region originally known in the 1970s for aromatic Riesling; Ancient Lakes crisp citrus whites | Everett Herald (Great Northwest Wine): cooler Yakima Valley and Ancient Lakes particularly suited; Spätlese style, medium dry and late harvest examples | Washington State Wine: Riesling a top variety

value: One of the valley's two main white grapes alongside Riesling, grown widely across the basin.
source_notes: Washington State Wine: top varieties Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Merlot, Riesling, Syrah (the only whites are Chardonnay and Riesling); Chardonnay a top variety on Wahluke Slope | Wine Folly: Chardonnay associated with Yakima Valley, Horse Heaven Hills, Ancient Lakes, Rattlesnake Hills
